stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a new phone app reduces evening screen time. They have 60 volunteer students available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of reaction time (hundredths of a second) are:

**Morning:** 11, 12, 14, 14, 17, 18, 19, 20, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 27

**Evening:** 16, 16, 23, 24, 26, 28, 29, 34, 35, 35, 37, 40, 43, 44, 72
A school district claims that 60% of its students take public transit to school. A reporter suspects the true proportion is higher. In a random sample of 320 students, 214 take public transit.

Data were collected on outdoor temperature (°F) (x) and daily iced-drink sales (y) for a sample of days. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    54.8
x           2.6
S = 5.5    R-Sq = 60.0%
```

questions.stem: In a random sample of 590 teenagers in a state, 271 get at least 8 hours of sleep. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all teenagers in a state who get at least 8 hours of sleep?

options.why: Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Divide by n inside the square root.
Multiply the standard error by z*.
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.96.

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 26 + 0.7x. An observation has x = 16 and y = 43.1. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.why: That is the predicted value ŷ.

options.text: 5.9; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.

options.text: 5.9; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.

options.text: -5.9; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.

questions.stem: The data are: 10, 20, 20, 23, 23, 26, 32, 33, 33, 35, 36, 56. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 21.5, Q3 = 34; values above 52.8 are outliers, so 56 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 12.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 52.8.

options.text: Q1 = 21.5, Q3 = 34; values above 47.8 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 21.5, Q3 = 34; values above 46.5 are outliers, so 56 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

questions.stem: For a distribution of time spent on homework, the mean is 64 and the median is 78. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.

questions.explanation: Mean 64 < median 78: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 55 and standard deviation 16. What proportion of values are less than 40.6?

options.why: That is the other side of the boundary.
Use the normal distribution's area, not the z-score.
Divide by σ when standardizing.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for p is (0.42, 0.51). Which claim is supported?

options.text: Exactly 46.5% of the population has the trait
options.why: The center is an estimate.

options.text: The population proportion must be greater than 0.5
options.why: Most of the interval is below 0.5.

options.text: There is a 95% probability that p is between 0.42 and 0.51
options.why: The probability statement applies to the method, not this interval.

options.text: It is plausible that fewer than half the population has the trait
options.why: Correct. Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

questions.explanation: Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

questions.stem: Each of 20 students takes a reading test before and after a summer program. Which procedure compares the scores?

options.text: A paired t procedure on the differences (after − before)
options.why: Correct. Two measurements on the same students are paired.
That is for categorical data.
The samples are not independent.
Scores are quantitative.

questions.explanation: Two measurements on the same students are paired.

questions.stem: Which variable is quantitative?

options.text: The number of text messages a student sends per day
options.why: Correct. Counts are quantitative.
That is categorical.

options.text: Whether a student owns a car (yes or no)
options.why: That is categorical.
Zip codes are labels.

questions.stem: A regression of weight (kg) on height (cm) for children aged 5–10 is used to predict the weight of an adult who is 180 cm tall. What is the main problem?

options.text: Extrapolation beyond the range of the data
options.why: Correct. The pattern may not hold for adults.
Height and weight are positively related.
It is quantitative.
Unrelated.

questions.explanation: The pattern may not hold for adults.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A and B) = 0.09. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.18.
P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.18.
Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.
That is P(drives | junior).
That is P(junior) overall.
Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.

questions.stem: In an experiment on a new reading program, students are first grouped by reading level, then randomly assigned to programs within each level. What is the purpose of grouping by level?

options.text: Blocking, to reduce variability caused by reading level
options.why: Correct. Blocking controls a known source of variation.
It remains an experiment.
Groups by level are not placebo groups.
That is a sampling idea.

questions.explanation: Blocking controls a known source of variation.

questions.stem: Each of 4 independent devices fails with probability 0.15. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: That is the probability none fail.
That is the probability all fail.
Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂ is (−2.4, 5.1). What can be concluded?

options.why: Negative differences are also plausible.
Positive differences are also plausible.

options.text: The two means are exactly equal
options.why: The interval does not prove equality.

options.text: There is no convincing evidence of a difference in population means, because 0 is in the interval
options.why: Correct. Zero is a plausible difference.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.
That is the largest probability, not the mean.
Weight each value by its probability.
Correct. μ = Σ x·P(x).

questions.stem: The correlation between hours studied and exam score is r = 0.6. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: Hours studied causes 36% of exam score
options.why: Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 60% of the variation in exam score is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.

options.text: About 36% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

options.text: About 36% of the variation in exam score is accounted for by the linear model relating exam score to hours studied
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 34, s₁ = 8 and n₂ = 23, s₂ = 12. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Each sample contributes s²/n.
Variances add, even for a difference.

questions.stem: For a distribution of household incomes in a city, the mean is 57 and the median is 42. Which is the most likely shape?

questions.stem: Why is the t distribution used instead of the normal distribution for inference about a mean?

options.text: Because σ is estimated by s, which adds variability
options.why: Correct. t has heavier tails to account for it.

options.text: Because t is used only for proportions
options.why: It is used for means.

options.text: Because the sample is always biased
options.why: Bias is unrelated.

options.text: Because sample means are never normal
options.why: They often are approximately normal.

questions.explanation: t has heavier tails to account for it.

questions.stem: Does increasing the sample size reduce bias in a survey?

options.text: No; a larger sample reduces variability but not bias from the sampling method
options.why: Correct. Bias is systematic.

options.text: Yes; large samples are always unbiased
options.why: A biased method stays biased.
Size never fixes bias.

options.text: Yes, if the sample is over 1,000
options.why: Size does not fix a biased method.

options.why: a = ȳ − b·x̄.
Correct. b = r·sy/sx and a = ȳ − b·x̄.
Multiply sy/sx by r.
The slope is r·sy/sx, not r·sx/sy.

options.why: Correct. SRSs within groups (strata).
Cluster sampling selects whole groups.

questions.stem: Researchers recruited 200 volunteers among students at the school and randomly assigned them to use one of two study apps, then compared test scores. Can the researchers conclude that the app causes higher scores, and to whom do the results apply?

options.text: No to cause and effect, but the association can be generalized to all students at the school
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, but only for the volunteers in the study
options.why: Correct. Random assignment decides causation; no random selection decides generalization.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, and yes to generalizing to all students at the school
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: No to cause and effect, and no generalization beyond the volunteers
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

questions.explanation: Random assignment: yes. Random selection: no.

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the app lead to a better average evening screen time over two weeks than no app for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the app vs no app). Response: average evening screen time over two weeks.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 60 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–60; use a random number generator to select 30 different numbers.
Those 30 receive the app; the remaining 30 receive no app.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by grade level (9th and 12th graders use phones differently). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by grade level.

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.

rubric.example: IQR = 16; upper fence = 40 + 1.5(16) = 64. Outlier(s): 72.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for Evening (34) is greater than for Morning (20).
Evening is more variable (IQR 16 vs 9).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: Evening has a high outlier, suggesting right skew.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for Evening, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 33.5 is pulled toward the high value; median 34 is not.

parts.prompt: State the hypotheses, defining the parameter.

rubric.criterion: Correct hypotheses with the parameter defined.
rubric.example: H₀: p = 0.6; Hₐ: p > 0.6, where p is the proportion of all district students who take public transit.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate procedure and check its conditions.

rubric.criterion: One-sample z test for a proportion.
rubric.example: Random sample stated.
320 is less than 10% of all students (assumed); np₀ = 192 and n(1 − p₀) = 128 are both at least 10.

parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
State a conclusion in context at α = 0.05.

rubric.criterion: Correct decision linked to the p-value, in context.
rubric.example: Because 0.006 is less than 0.05, reject H₀: convincing evidence that the proportion is greater than 0.6.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 54.8 + 2.6x, where ŷ is predicted daily iced-drink sales and x is outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of outdoor temperature (°F), the predicted daily iced-drink sales increases by about 2.6.
About 60.0% of the variation in daily iced-drink sales is accounted for by the linear model with outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 13 and y = 90.9. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 88.6; residual = 90.9 − 88.6 = 2.3: the actual value is above the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of days from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
